summary.prose: Chat sessions move out of VS Code's globalState, where every save rewrites one 29.6 MB value, into two files per session under ~/.insrc/chat-sessions: a small head and a transcript file with one row per line. A save appends only the rows that session object has not yet written and replaces the head, so its cost no longer grows with the history, and the history list reads heads only. The store's interface and its callers do not change. Sessions already in globalState are copied to files once, checked, and only then removed from it.

hldContextSlice.frameworkSummary: Standalone feature — no parent HLD. Design directly against the repo, grounded on the s1 analyze passes. There are no HLD shared contracts to honour.

boundary.internal: Store chat sessions in files so a save writes only what changed

api.name: ChatSessionStore
api.signature: interface ChatSessionStore { create(provider: ProviderId): ChatSession; draft(provider: ProviderId): ChatSession; get(id: string): ChatSession | undefined; list(): ReadonlyArray<ChatSummary>; append(id: string, entry: TranscriptEntry): void; save(session: ChatSession): void }

returns.meaning: Unchanged. The existing synchronous interface; the new file store implements it, so chat-panel.ts and turn-lifecycle.ts are not edited.

errors.condition: save() throws when a file cannot be written; trySaveSession already catches and logs it.

postconditions: get() never throws: a missing or unreadable session is undefined.
list() never throws: an unreadable head is left out.

api.name: createFileChatSessionStore
api.signature: function createFileChatSessionStore(deps: FileStoreDeps): ChatSessionStore  // NEW, in vscode-plugin/src/chat/session-file-store.ts. interface FileStoreDeps { readonly root: string; readonly fs?: SessionFilesFs; readonly now?: () => string; readonly genId?: () => string; readonly maxSessions?: number; readonly onEvict?: ((sessionId: string) => void) | undefined; readonly logger?: { warn(msg: string): void } }

parameters.name: deps.root
parameters.purpose: The directory holding the session files; extension.ts passes join(PATHS.insrc, 'chat-sessions').

parameters.name: deps.fs
parameters.purpose: The synchronous file seam; node's fs by default, an in-memory fake in tests.

parameters.name: deps.maxSessions
parameters.purpose: The session cap, with the same meaning as today: only a positive integer is a cap.

parameters.name: deps.onEvict
parameters.purpose: Called with the id of each session evicted beyond the cap, as today.

returns.meaning: A store whose sessions are `<root>/<sessionFileName(id)>.head.json` and `<root>/<sessionFileName(id)>.rows.ndjson`.

preconditions: sessionFileName from session-output.ts names the files, so a session's files and its output files share a base name.
postconditions: TRACKING. For every session object the store hands out (get, draft, create) or is given to save, it keeps the number of that object's leading rows that are on disk: the rows read for get, 0 for draft, the transcript's length after each successful save. The count belongs to the OBJECT, not the id, and is kept for as long as the object lives. Neither another window's append nor a get() that returns a fresh object for the same id removes or changes it.

save(s) for a tracked object appends to the rows file exactly the rows of s.transcript beyond its count, then replaces the head through a temporary file and a rename. So an object the callers hold and save again and again (turn-lifecycle.ts cursor tracker, chat-panel.ts `session`) only ever appends, whatever else has happened to the files.

The rows file is replaced whole (temporary file and rename) in two cases only, neither of which the callers reach: an object the store has NEVER tracked saved for an id whose files exist, and a tracked object whose transcript is shorter than its count.
The head is written after the rows, so a session that has a head has its rows. The head is last-writer-wins between windows.

SEVERAL WINDOWS. The store also keeps, per id, the rows file's size as it last left or read it. When the size found before an append differs, another writer appended: this object's new rows are still appended after theirs, the head is written, the recorded size is updated, and the store drops only the id's cached object, so the next get(id) reads the files and returns a fresh object holding every row in file order. File order is the order of the saves: each window's rows keep their own order and the two windows' rows interleave by save time.

get(id) returns the same object on repeated calls while the head's modification time and the rows file's size are as this store last left them; otherwise it reads the files again and returns a fresh, separately tracked object. The older object stays tracked.
A rows file whose last line is incomplete (no trailing newline, or not JSON) is read without that line and cut back to the last complete line before anything is appended.
list() reads heads only and sorts by updatedAt descending, as today.

When a save creates a new head and more than maxSessions heads exist, the heads with the oldest savedAt are removed with their rows files and onEvict is called for each; the session being saved is never removed.
draft() writes nothing; create() saves at once, as today.

api.name: SessionFilesFs
api.signature: interface SessionFilesFs { mkdir(dir: string): void; readText(path: string): string | undefined; writeText(path: string, data: string): void; appendText(path: string, data: string): void; rename(from: string, to: string): void; remove(path: string): void; truncate(path: string, bytes: number): void; stat(path: string): { readonly size: number; readonly mtimeMs: number } | undefined; list(dir: string): string[] }  // NEW; export const nodeSessionFilesFs: SessionFilesFs

returns.meaning: The synchronous file calls the store needs, kept structural so tests inject a fake, as SessionOutputFs does for the output files.

errors.condition: writeText, appendText, rename and truncate throw on failure; readText and stat return undefined for a missing file; list returns [] for a missing directory.

api.name: migrateChatSessionsFromMemento
api.signature: function migrateChatSessionsFromMemento(deps: { readonly memento: MementoLike; readonly root: string; readonly fs?: SessionFilesFs; readonly logger?: { warn(msg: string): void; info?(msg: string): void } }): { readonly migrated: number; readonly kept: readonly string[] }  // NEW, in session-file-store.ts

parameters.name: deps.memento
parameters.purpose: context.globalState, read through the existing `insrc.chat.index` and `insrc.chat.session.<id>` keys.

parameters.name: deps.root
parameters.purpose: The same directory the file store uses.

returns.meaning: How many sessions were moved to files and removed from the memento, and the ids of the sessions left in it. extension.ts adds the kept ids to the output sweep's keep set, so a session still waiting in globalState does not lose its output files.

preconditions: Called once at activation, before the file store is built and before the output sweep.
postconditions: For each indexed session that isSession accepts: when no head exists, its rows file and then its head are written through temporary files and renames; when a head exists and the files' rows are a prefix of the memento's rows, the missing rows are appended; when the memento's rows are a prefix of the files' rows nothing is written.

The files are then read back and compared with the memento's session (every row and every head field). Only when they match, or the files hold the memento's rows as a prefix, is `insrc.chat.session.<id>` set to undefined.

A session whose files and memento copy disagree in any other way, whose write or read-back fails, or that isSession rejects, is left in the memento untouched, logged, and returned in `kept`; it is tried again at the next start.
`insrc.chat.index` is rewritten to the kept ids, or set to undefined when none were kept.
Never throws; with no index it does nothing and returns { migrated: 0, kept: [] }.

returns.meaning: Unchanged and kept: createInMemoryChatSessionStore (the tests' store) is built on it, and its key names are what the migration reads. extension.ts stops constructing it.

errorCases.scenario: A save cannot write (disk full, directory not writable).
errorCases.detection: appendText, writeText or rename throws inside save().
errorCases.response: save() lets the error out; trySaveSession logs it. The object's count is advanced only after its append succeeded, so rows that were not written are tried again by the next save and rows that were written are never written twice. A rows append that succeeded before a failing head write is kept: a read takes its rows from the rows file, not from the head's count.
errorCases.userImpact: The turn carries on; the rows are saved by a later save, or lost if every later save fails too.

errorCases.scenario: The process dies in the middle of appending rows.
errorCases.detection: On the next read the rows file's last line has no trailing newline or is not JSON.
errorCases.response: The read leaves that line out and cuts the file back to the end of the last complete line, so later appends start on a clean line.
errorCases.userImpact: At most the rows of the interrupted save are missing.

errorCases.scenario: A head file is damaged or is not a session head.
errorCases.detection: It is not valid JSON, or fails the field checks (id, provider, createdAt, title, editMode).
errorCases.response: get() returns undefined and list() leaves it out; nothing is deleted. A warning is logged once per file.
errorCases.userImpact: That chat is missing from the history; its files remain on disk.

errorCases.scenario: A rows file holds a line in its middle that is not JSON.
errorCases.detection: JSON.parse throws on a line that is not the last.
errorCases.response: The line is skipped and logged; the other rows are returned in order. The file is not rewritten.
errorCases.userImpact: One row of that chat is missing.

errorCases.scenario: Another window appended to a session this window also holds.
errorCases.detection: Before a save's append, the rows file's size is not the size this store recorded for that id after its last read or write.
errorCases.response: This object's new rows are appended after the other window's rows, the head is written and the recorded size is updated. The object stays tracked with its own count, so every later save of it (the cursor tracker's, the panel's, and the save after chat-panel.ts 1065's get) still only appends its new rows. Only the id's cached object is dropped, so the next get() reads the files and returns a fresh object with every row in file order.
errorCases.userImpact: No row of either window is lost and no file is replaced. The panel showing the older object keeps its own view until the chat is opened again, and the two windows' rows appear in the order they were saved.

errorCases.scenario: The migration cannot write or verify a session.
errorCases.detection: A file call throws, or the session read back from the files differs from the memento's copy.
errorCases.response: The memento entry is left exactly as it was, the id stays in the index and is returned in `kept`, a warning names the session, and the migration goes on with the next one. extension.ts keeps that id's output files out of the sweep.
errorCases.userImpact: That chat is still in globalState and not in the history until a later start migrates it; its output files are not removed meanwhile.

errorCases.scenario: A memento session and its files disagree (neither is a prefix of the other).
errorCases.detection: The migration compares the rows pairwise up to the shorter length and finds a difference.
errorCases.response: Neither copy is changed; the memento entry is kept, the id is returned in `kept`, and a warning is logged.
errorCases.userImpact: The history shows the files' copy; the other copy stays in globalState.

errorCases.scenario: Removing an evicted session's files fails.
errorCases.response: The error is logged, onEvict is still called for that id, and the save that triggered the eviction succeeds.
errorCases.userImpact: None; a stale file may remain.

migration.stateBefore: Sessions live in VS Code's globalState, one key per session with the transcript inline and an index key (s1: symbol.locate). VS Code stores all of the extension's keys as one value, measured at 29.6 MB for three sessions (s1: search.text), so each save rewrites all of it, up to every 500 ms during a turn (s1: usage.example, how callers hold and save a session).
migration.stateAfter: Sessions live in ~/.insrc/chat-sessions as a head file and a rows file each. globalState holds no chat session and no chat index once every session has been migrated. A save appends new rows and replaces a small head.

migrationSteps.action: Add the file store and the migration function beside the memento store, with their tests. Nothing uses them yet.

At activation, run the migration before the store is built: copy each indexed session to files, read it back, and compare it with the memento's copy. Up to this point globalState is unchanged, so going back to the previous plugin version loses nothing.

For each session that verified, remove its key from globalState; rewrite the index to the kept ids, or remove it. From here the previous plugin version no longer sees the migrated chats; they remain in the files.

Build the chat store from the file store in extension.ts, with the same cap and the same onEvict, and give the output sweep the store's ids plus the ids the migration kept. Update the wiring test's pinned text and the two comments that say sessions live in globalState.
On every later activation the migration runs again and finds nothing, or picks up sessions a window on the previous version wrote to globalState in the meantime.

migration.backwardCompat: No public API changes: ChatSessionStore is unchanged. The stored location changes. A window still running the previous plugin version keeps reading and writing globalState: it does not see chats migrated by a newer window, and what it writes is migrated at the next start of a newer window (rows appended when the files hold a prefix of them, kept in globalState when the copies disagree). Installing the previous version after step 3 shows an empty history until the newer version is installed again; the files are not touched by it.

alternativesConsidered.name: Head file plus append-only rows file, synchronous
alternativesConsidered.oneLineSummary: Each session is two files under ~/.insrc/chat-sessions: a small head written whole and a rows file that a save only appends to.
alternativesConsidered.approach: A new file-backed ChatSessionStore keeps `<name>.head.json` (every ChatSession field except the transcript) and `<name>.rows.ndjson` (one transcript row per line). The store remembers, for each session object it has handed out or saved, how many of that object's rows are on disk; a save appends the rest and replaces the head through a temporary file and a rename. list() reads heads only. File access is synchronous through an injected seam, so the interface and its callers are unchanged. Sessions in globalState are copied to files once at start, read back, and only then removed.
pros: A save writes the new rows and a small head, whatever the history's length.
The history list reads no transcript.
The store interface and both callers stay as they are.
Frees the 29.6 MB value VS Code rewrites on every update of any key.
A crash mid-append can only damage the last line.
cons: Synchronous file calls on the extension host, each small after the first read.
The first get() of a long session still reads and parses its whole rows file.
Chat history moves from VS Code's storage to the user's home directory, like the output files.

alternativesConsidered.name: Same files, asynchronous store
alternativesConsidered.oneLineSummary: The same two files, but every store method returns a promise and writes are queued per session.
alternativesConsidered.approach: The file layout of a1 with ChatSessionStore made asynchronous: get, list and save return promises and a per-session queue keeps writes in order. chat-panel.ts and turn-lifecycle.ts await the store wherever they read or save a session.
pros: No synchronous file call on the extension host.
cons: Changes the interface and every caller; the panel's write-before-post order would have to be rebuilt across awaits.
A failed queued write can no longer be reported at the call that caused it.
A much larger change for a cost a1 already makes small.
alternativesConsidered.reasonRejected: Same result on disk, but it rewrites the callers and their tests to remove synchronous calls that a1 already keeps small. Worth revisiting only if the first read of a very long session proves too slow in practice.

alternativesConsidered.name: Keep globalState, save less often
alternativesConsidered.oneLineSummary: Leave sessions in globalState and reduce how often they are saved.
alternativesConsidered.approach: Keep the memento store and cut the number of updates: a longer cursor interval, and one save per turn at its end, with the cursor in a separate small key.
pros: Smallest change; no migration and no new files.
cons: Every remaining update still rewrites the whole 29.6 MB value, because all keys are one stored value.
Saving less often loses more on a crash or reload mid-turn.
The history list still reads every transcript.
alternativesConsidered.reasonRejected: Does not fix the defect: fewer saves of the same size, and more lost on a crash.
